title: Nilkanth's walk to Loj
hookLine: a boy with a staff and a loincloth walks out of his village and keeps walking until he reaches Gujarat
carry: a seeker's road leads to a guru
tomorrow: what happened at Loj, and what name came after?

cards: Bare feet on a mountain path, high in the Himalayas. A boy, thin from fasting, wearing only a loincloth, carrying a staff, a string of beads and a small bundle. No family with him.
In the stories his followers tell, he left home young, and he's been walking ever since, from one holy place to the next, looking for something. People along the road call him Nilkanth.
Today, a new region, Gujarat, and the walk that brought this boy there.

teach.b: Tradition says he was born Ghanshyam, in a village called Chhapaiya, not far from Ayodhya in the north.
After his parents died, he left home as a young renunciant, a brahmachari, and took the name Nilkanth, blue-throat, one of the names of Shiva.
His followers tell of a long journey on foot across India: the Himalayas, the holy sites of the east, the temples of the south, hard austerities, yogi after yogi, and moving on from each.
He wasn't wandering for its own sake. He was asking questions and not settling for half answers.
At last he comes west, into Gujarat, to a small ashram at a village called Loj. It belongs to a teacher named Ramanand Swami, and his disciple Muktanand receives the young stranger.

Nilkanth asks his questions: about the soul, about God, about the world and what binds us to it. Followers tell that the answers satisfied him, and this time he stays. Here's the teaching under the walk.
In Hinduism the deepest knowledge is received from a guru. The Mundaka Upanishad tells the seeker to go, fuel for the fire in hand, to a teacher who knows the scriptures and stands firm in Brahman.
That's the seed of the Swaminarayan tradition, a living Hindu community with deep roots in Gujarat.
And it's why so many Hindu families still say: for the questions that matter most, don't stop at the first answer you find. Find someone who has walked the road, and learn at their feet.

how: Swaminarayan followers tell the story of Nilkanth Varni's journey on foot across India, and their temples may show the young yogi standing on one leg in austerity, with his staff and beads.

o: a Gujarat tradition of priests who never leave their temple
a Gujarat tradition that began with a wandering boy yogi
a Gujarat tradition founded by a king who left his throne

s: the Mundaka Upanishad tells a seeker to go to a teacher who stands firm in Brahman
it says to go, fuel in hand, to a guru who knows the scriptures and is rooted in Brahman: the road Nilkanth walked.
Nilkanth was wandering just to see the world
he was asking questions about the soul and God, and not settling for half answers.
at Loj, Nilkanth was received by Muktanand, a disciple of Ramanand Swami
the ashram was Ramanand Swami's, and Muktanand received the young stranger there.

games.q: you're Nilkanth. you've walked for a long time, met teacher after teacher, and moved on from each. you reach a small ashram at Loj and ask your questions. what do you do?
games.why: this time he stays: he's found answers he can trust, and the Swaminarayan tradition begins there.

practice: Sit tall, as if you had a staff in your hand, and let a real question come up, one you haven't finished with, about God, about yourself, about what matters.

Don't answer it; let it walk with you, breath after breath, the way Nilkanth carried his questions from place to place. If you pray, hold the question as a prayer, and ask to be led to the right teacher.

wordCard.voice: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, Nilkanth: the boy born Ghanshyam, who walked across India with his questions until he reached Ramanand Swami's ashram at Loj. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: 'blue-throat', a name of Shiva, taken by the boy Ghanshyam as he walked.
